title: Speed and Distance–Time Graphs
summary: How to calculate speed, distance and time, find average speeds, and read, draw and interpret distance–time graphs — with worked examples and a Checkpoint-style quiz.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Calculate speed using speed = distance ÷ time, and rearrange it to find distance or time. (8Pf.01)
Read and explain simple distance–time graphs, and draw them from data. (8Pf.02)

blocks.text: 1. Key words

items: speed
السرعة — how far something travels in each second (or hour)
distance
المسافة — how far something travels, in m or km
time
الزمن — how long the journey takes, in s, min or h
average speed
السرعة المتوسطة — total distance ÷ total time for the whole journey
constant speed
سرعة ثابتة — the same distance is covered every second
stationary
ساكن / واقف — not moving
accelerate
يتسارع — speed up
decelerate
يتباطأ — slow down
distance–time graph
منحنى المسافة والزمن — a graph of distance (up) against time (across)
gradient
الميل — how steep a line is; on a distance–time graph it gives the speed
metres per second (m/s)
متر لكل ثانية — the SI unit of speed

blocks.text: 2. What is speed?

**Speed** tells you how fast something is moving: how much **distance** it covers in each unit of **time**. A car moving at 20 m/s travels 20 metres every second. To find a speed you need two measurements: the distance travelled and the time taken.

blocks.title: The formula
blocks.text: **speed = distance ÷ time**   (in symbols: s = d ÷ t)

rows: **kilometres per hour (km/h)** — used for cars and trains
**centimetres per second (cm/s)** — for small, slow things

blocks.text: **Rearranging.** You can use the same three quantities to find distance or time. The formula triangle helps: cover the quantity you want and the triangle shows the calculation.

blocks.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 480 225" width="480" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16"><polygon points="240,20 110,210 370,210" fill="#fff4d6" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="162" y1="135" x2="318" y2="135" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="2"/><text x="240" y="108" text-anchor="middle" font-size="30" font-weight="bold">d</text><text x="190" y="190" text-anchor="middle" font-size="30" font-weight="bold">s</text><text x="290" y="190" text-anchor="middle" font-size="30" font-weight="bold">t</text><text x="240" y="188" text-anchor="middle" font-size="30">×</text></svg>
blocks.caption: Formula triangle: d = distance, s = speed, t = time. Cover d: d = s × t. Cover s: s = d ÷ t. Cover t: t = d ÷ s.

blocks.text: 3. Units: change them first
Before you calculate, make the units match. If the question asks for m/s, the distance must be in **metres** and the time in **seconds**.

items: 1 minute = **60 s**   (minutes → seconds: × 60)
1 hour = 60 minutes = **3600 s**
30 minutes = 0.5 h; 15 minutes = 0.25 h; 20 minutes = 1/3 h

blocks.text: 4. Average speed
Real journeys are never at one steady speed: cars stop at traffic lights and speed up again. **Average speed** treats the whole journey as if it were at one steady speed:

blocks.title: Average speed
blocks.text: **average speed = total distance travelled ÷ total time taken** — the total time **includes** any time spent stopped.
A speedometer shows the speed at one instant. An average speed can be much lower, because of the stops.

**Measuring speed in the laboratory.** To find the speed of a toy car: mark a start and a finish line a measured distance apart (for example 2.00 m, with a metre rule or tape measure); time the car between the lines with a stopwatch; **repeat** three times and calculate a mean time; then speed = distance ÷ mean time. Human reaction time makes stopwatch timings less accurate, especially for short times — **light gates** connected to a timer are more accurate.

blocks.title: احفظ القانون
items: السرعة = المسافة ÷ الزمن. المسافة = السرعة × الزمن. الزمن = المسافة ÷ السرعة.
قبل ما تحسب، وحّد الوحدات: كيلومتر × 1000 = متر، دقيقة × 60 = ثانية.
السرعة المتوسطة = المسافة الكلية ÷ الزمن الكلي — وده بيشمل وقت الوقوف كمان.

blocks.text: 5. Distance–time graphs

A **distance–time graph** shows a journey as a picture. **Time** goes along the horizontal axis (x-axis) and **distance** goes up the vertical axis (y-axis). The **shape** of the line tells you how the object is moving.

items: **Start to A:** the line slopes up steadily — constant speed. Speed = 100 m ÷ 20 s = **5 m/s**.
**A to B:** the line is flat — the cyclist is **stationary** for 30 − 20 = 10 s.
**C to D:** flat — stationary again.
**Average speed** for the whole 60 s = 300 m ÷ 60 s = **5 m/s**.

blocks.text: 6. Drawing a distance–time graph

items: Put **time** on the x-axis and **distance** on the y-axis (time is the independent variable).
Label each axis with the quantity **and the unit**, e.g. "time in s", "distance in m".
Choose a **simple, even scale** (1, 2, 5 or 10 per square) that uses more than half of the grid. Start both axes at 0.
Plot each point accurately with a small cross (×).
Join the points with straight lines using a **ruler** if the object moves at steady speeds; draw a smooth curve if the speed is changing.

blocks.title: قراءة الرسم البياني
items: الخط الأفقي = الجسم واقف. الخط المايل المستقيم = سرعة ثابتة، وكل ما يكون أميل (أشد انحدارًا) تكون السرعة أكبر.
المنحنى اللي بيزيد ميله = بيسرّع، واللي ميله بيقل = بيبطّأ.
السرعة من الرسم = فرق المسافة ÷ فرق الزمن (مش القراءة نفسها).

blocks.text: 7. Worked examples
**Worked example 1** — A cheetah runs 210 m in 7 s. Calculate its speed. [2]

items: Write the formula: speed = distance ÷ time.
Substitute: speed = 210 ÷ 7.
Answer with unit: **30 m/s**.
**Common mistake:** writing 7 ÷ 210 = 0.033. Always distance **on top**.

blocks.alt: A cheetah running fast across grass
blocks.caption: A cheetah is the fastest land animal: in a short sprint it can reach about 30 m/s, which is over 100 km/h.
blocks.credit: Photo: Mark Dumont / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0

blocks.text: **Worked example 2** — A car moves at a constant 25 m/s for 40 s. How far does it travel? [2]

items: distance = speed × time

blocks.text: **Worked example 3** — An aeroplane flies 2400 km at an average speed of 800 km/h. How long does the flight take? [2]

items: time = distance ÷ speed
= **3 hours** (the units km and km/h give hours)

blocks.text: **Worked example 4** — Layla walks 900 m in 12 minutes. Calculate her average speed in m/s. [3]

items: Convert the time: 12 minutes × 60 = **720 s** (1).
**Common mistake:** 900 ÷ 12 = 75 — that is 75 metres per **minute**, not m/s.

blocks.text: **Worked example 5** — Use the cyclist graph in section 5. (a) Describe the motion between A and B. [1] (b) Which part of the journey is fastest? Explain how you can tell. [2]

items: (a) The cyclist is **stationary** (stopped) for 10 s — the line is horizontal.
(b) **B to C** (1), because that line is the **steepest** (1). (Check: 10 m/s compared with 5 m/s.)

blocks.text: **Worked example 6** — A ball rolls down a slope. Its distance–time graph is a curve that gets steeper. Then it rolls along a flat floor and its graph becomes a curve that gets flatter until it is horizontal. Describe the motion. [3]

items: Down the slope: the ball is **speeding up** (the line gets steeper) (1).
On the floor: the ball is **slowing down** (the line gets less steep) (1)…
…until it **stops** (horizontal line) (1).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Dividing the wrong way: speed = **distance ÷ time**, never time ÷ distance.
Mixing units: km with seconds, or minutes when the answer must be in m/s. Convert first.
Forgetting the unit, or writing the wrong one (m/s for speed, m for distance, s for time).
Leaving out the stopped time when working out an average speed.
Reading values instead of changes: for a section of a graph, use (distance at end − distance at start) ÷ (time at end − time at start).
Thinking a horizontal line means "constant speed". Flat means **not moving**.
Drawing a 'dot-to-dot' freehand line or a curve through points that lie on a straight line — use a ruler.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: **Calculate** a speed, distance or time — write the formula, substitute, answer, unit. Each step can earn a mark.
**Average speed** for a journey in stages, often with a stop and a change of units.
**Read a graph**: distance at a time, how long the object stopped, which part is fastest.
**Calculate speed from a graph** section using changes in distance and time.
**Describe** a section of a graph: stationary / constant speed / speeding up / slowing down / returning.
**Plot** a distance–time graph from a table: labelled axes with units, even scale, accurate points, ruler lines.
**Method**: how to measure speed (distance with a metre rule or tape, time with a stopwatch or light gates, repeat and average).

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Speed and distance–time graphs — practice
blocks.intro: Answer every part. Type short answers in the box; for longer answers write yours on paper first, then mark it with the mark scheme.

questions.q: A car travels 600 m in 30 s. Calculate its speed. Give the unit.
questions.e: speed = distance ÷ time = 600 ÷ 30 = **20 m/s**. (1 mark for the calculation, 1 mark for the unit m/s — distance in m and time in s give speed in m/s.)

questions.q: A runner keeps a steady speed of 8 m/s for 15 s. How far does she run?
questions.e: distance = speed × time = 8 × 15 = **120 m**. Cover d in the triangle: s and t are side by side, so multiply.

questions.q: Omar walks 1.2 km to school in 10 minutes. Calculate his average speed in **m/s**. Show your working.
questions.e: Change the units first: 1.2 km = 1.2 × 1000 = 1200 m; 10 minutes = 10 × 60 = 600 s. Speed = 1200 ÷ 600 = **2 m/s**. Common mistake: 1.2 ÷ 10 = 0.12 — that is in km per minute, not m/s.

questions.q: What does a horizontal (flat) line on a distance–time graph show?
c: The object is moving at a constant speed.
The object is moving back to the start.
questions.e: A flat line means the **distance stays the same** as time goes on, so the object is **stationary**. A sloping straight line shows constant speed, and a line sloping down shows movement back towards the start.

questions.q: On a distance–time graph, the line is a curve that gets **steeper and steeper**. What is the object doing?
questions.e: The steepness (gradient) of a distance–time graph is the **speed**. If the line gets steeper, the speed is increasing, so the object is **speeding up**. A curve that gets flatter shows slowing down.

questions.e: Distance travelled = 350 − 150 = 200 m. Time taken = 200 − 150 = 50 s. Speed = 200 ÷ 50 = **4 m/s**. Common mistake: using the readings themselves (350 ÷ 200 = 1.75) instead of the **changes** in distance and time.

questions.q: (e) Describe the student's motion between D and E. [2]
questions.ms: 1 mark: moving back towards home / distance from home decreasing / returning. 1 mark: at a constant (steady) speed — accept a correct speed of 3.5 m/s, or 'arrives home at 300 s'. Do not accept 'slowing down' or 'going downhill'.
questions.e: The line slopes **down**, so the distance from home is getting smaller — the student is **walking back home**. The line is **straight**, so the speed is **constant**: 350 m in 100 s = 3.5 m/s. The student reaches home (0 m) at 300 s.

questions.q: (f) Calculate the student's average speed for the whole trip from A to E. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
questions.e: Total distance = 150 m (A–B) + 0 (B–C) + 200 m (C–D) + 350 m (D–E) = **700 m**. Total time = **300 s** (including the stop). Average speed = 700 ÷ 300 = **2.33 m/s**. Common mistake: using 0 m because the student ends at home — the distance **travelled** is 700 m, even though the final distance from home is 0.

questions.p:
Question 12
A student times a toy car rolling along the floor. The table shows the results.
time in s | 0 | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 | 10
distance in m | 0 | 1.0 | 2.0 | 3.0 | 3.0 | 3.0
questions.q: (a) Draw a distance–time graph of these results on graph paper. [3]
questions.ms: 1 mark: time on the x-axis and distance on the y-axis, both labelled with units (s, m). 1 mark: sensible linear scales using more than half the grid (e.g. 1 cm = 1 s, 1 cm = 0.5 m) and all 6 points plotted correctly to within half a small square. 1 mark: straight line drawn with a ruler from (0, 0) to (6, 3.0), then a horizontal line from (6, 3.0) to (10, 3.0). Do not accept a curve through the points or a dot-to-dot freehand line.
questions.e: Put **time (s)** across the bottom (x-axis) because it is the independent variable, and **distance (m)** up the side (y-axis). Choose even scales (for example 1 large square = 2 s across and 1 large square = 1 m up). Plot the six points with small crosses. The points from 0 s to 6 s lie on a straight line — draw it with a ruler. From 6 s to 10 s the distance stays at 3.0 m, so the line is horizontal: the car has stopped.

questions.p:
Question 12
A student times a toy car rolling along the floor. The table shows the results.
time in s | 0 | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 | 10
distance in m | 0 | 1.0 | 2.0 | 3.0 | 3.0 | 3.0
questions.q: (b) Calculate the speed of the toy car during the first 6 s.
questions.e: In the first 6 s the car travels 3.0 m. Speed = 3.0 ÷ 6 = **0.5 m/s**. (The same answer comes from any 2 s step: 1.0 m ÷ 2 s = 0.5 m/s, which shows the speed is constant.)

questions.q: A bus travels 20 km in 20 minutes on a motorway. It then travels 10 km in 30 minutes through a town. Calculate its average speed for the whole journey in **km/h**. Show your working.
questions.e: Total distance = 20 + 10 = **30 km** (1). Total time = 20 + 30 = 50 minutes = 50 ÷ 60 h = 5/6 h (1). Average speed = 30 ÷ 5/6 = 30 × 6 ÷ 5 = **36 km/h** (1). Check: at this rate, in 60 minutes the bus would go 30 × 60 ÷ 50 = 36 km. Common mistake: averaging the two speeds. The speeds are 60 km/h and 20 km/h, and (60 + 20) ÷ 2 = 40 km/h is **wrong**, because the bus spends longer at the slow speed. Always use total distance ÷ total time.

blocks.title: Remember
items: speed = distance ÷ time; distance = speed × time; time = distance ÷ speed.
Make units match before you calculate: m and s give m/s; km and h give km/h.
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time, including stops.
On a distance–time graph: flat = stationary, straight slope = constant speed, steeper = faster, curves = speeding up or slowing down.
Speed from a graph = change in distance ÷ change in time.
